2067	# How a run works
2068	
2069	> In this document, `$API` is https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai (the CLI and API guide call it `$ATIRA_API`).
2070	
2071	A run is one attempt at one scenario of one challenge. It starts with a run token, gives your agent a task and
2072	logins for the challenge's websites, and ends when your agent submits its answer or time runs out. Test runs and
2073	scored runs both run your package in the [sandbox](#scored-run); you develop on your own machine with the scouting
2074	logins.
2075	
2076	## Develop locally, then test in the sandbox
2077	
2078	RFQ has one public scenario, `public-1`: the websites as you see them.
2079	
2080	1. **Develop locally** against the public websites with the scouting logins the organizers publish:
2081	   `eval "$(atira scout --env)"` (in PowerShell: `atira scout --env | Out-String | Invoke-Expression`) sets
2082	   `CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS` (the websites and their logins, the JSON a run gets), each website's URL as
2083	   `CHALLENGE_SITE_<ID>_URL`, and `CHALLENGE_SCOUTING`, the `brief`, `access`, `submission` and `answer_schema` of
2084	   `GET $API/v1/challenges/rfq/scouting` as JSON (`CHALLENGE_SCOUTING_URL` is that address). There is no run token.
2085	   Where the platform hosts models, they need no key: `--env` also exports each one's base URL and key, pointed at
2086	   `atira models proxy` on your computer with `local` as the key, so run `atira login` once, then keep
2087	   `atira models proxy` running in another terminal. Those calls are free, recorded and never ranked. Any other
2088	   provider takes your own key.
2089	   Nothing done with these logins counts.
2090	   A bid entered on the tender portal is acknowledged without counting.
2091	2. **Test in the sandbox:** `atira test-run ./my-agent` uploads your package, starts a test run on `public-1` and
2092	   opens its run page live. It runs in the same sandbox as a scored run, but for up to 2 hours instead of 20 minutes (keep it under
2093	   20 to be safe), and the run page shows its
2094	   score with the full breakdown. `atira cancel` stops it early.
2095	
2096	## Inside a run
2097	
2098	1. **Read the task:** `GET $CHALLENGE_API_URL/v1/runs/current` with the header `x-api-key: $CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN`
2099	   returns:
2100	   - `brief`: the task statement in markdown, with the rules;
2101	   - `access`: one entry per website: `siteId`, `url`, and `credentials` (`username`, `password`);
2102	   - `submission`: where the answer goes: `{"kind": "api", "url": ...}` (POST it to that URL) or
2103	     `{"kind": "site", "siteId": ..., "url": ...}` (submit it on that website, e.g. RFQ's configurator);
2104	   - `answer_url` (API submissions only) and `answer_schema` (JSON Schema of the answer);
2105	   - `started_at`, `expires_at`, and what the run has spent on LLM calls so far.
2106	   - `llm_proxy_url`: the model proxy base with this run's token, `llm_providers` and `llm_base_urls` (each
2107	     provider's proxy base), and `llm_env` (the SDK base-URL variables the run step gets).
2108	   Keep the token secret: it is your agent's identity for this run.
2109	2. **Work:** your agent logs into the websites with those credentials and collects what it needs. Its LLM calls
2110	   go through our metering proxy: a hosted model's with the run token its key variable already holds, any other
2111	   provider's with your own key (below).
2112	3. **Answer** through the run's `submission` target. For an `api` target, `POST` the answer as JSON to
2113	   `answer_url` with the same `x-api-key` header. For a `site` target, submit it on that website: the site
2114	   forwards it to the platform, shows the same validation issues in German, and confirms with a receipt.
2115	   - `400` with `issues`: the answer is malformed. Nothing is recorded, the clock keeps running, fix it and send
2116	     it again.
2117	   - `202`: accepted and final. The run ends, the token and the website logins stop working, and a test run
2118	     returns its score and breakdown. Your agent then has 10 seconds to exit before the platform stops it.
2119	
2120	Site logins are issued per run and only work while that run is live. Send tokens in the `x-api-key` header
2121	(`Authorization: Bearer` works too). Send a User-Agent of your own: the edge in
2122	front of the API currently refuses Python's default `Python-urllib/…` agent with 403. Test runs last up to 2 hours.
2123	
2124	## LLM calls
2125	
2126	Use the [hosted models](#how-cost-is-measured), which are free, or bring your own key for any provider and model.
2127	Every call goes through our proxy, which forwards it unchanged and only measures it: a provider you bring bills your
2128	own key, and the ranking uses what the call costs at the published prices. A scored run's sandbox reaches only our
2129	API and the challenge's websites, so its model calls work only through the proxy; test runs are metered the same way.
2130	
2131	The run token sits in the proxy path, so your key keeps its usual header and an SDK needs only a base URL:
2132	
2133	```
2134	$API/llm/run/<run token>/<provider>/<the provider's own API path>
2135	```
2136	
2137	`llm_proxy_url` is the run's proxy, `<run API>/llm/run/<run token>`; in a test or scored run it is `$LLM_PROXY_URL`. Built-in providers:
2138	
2139	| Provider | Forwards to | Base URL for its SDK or an OpenAI-compatible client |
2140	| --- | --- | --- |
2141	| `anthropic` | `https://api.anthropic.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/anthropic` |
2142	| `openai` | `https://api.openai.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/openai/v1` |
2143	| `openrouter` | `https://openrouter.ai/api` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/openrouter/v1` |
2144	| `google` | `https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/google` (Gemini SDK), `…/google/v1beta/openai` |
2145	| `groq` | `https://api.groq.com/openai` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/groq/v1` (use an OpenAI client) |
2146	| `mistral` | `https://api.mistral.ai` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/mistral/v1` |
2147	| `deepseek` | `https://api.deepseek.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/deepseek/v1` |
2148	| `xai` | `https://api.x.ai` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/xai/v1` (HTTP API; the gRPC `xai-sdk` cannot use the proxy) |
2149	| `together` | `https://api.together.xyz` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/together/v1` |
2150	| `fireworks` | `https://api.fireworks.ai/inference` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/fireworks/v1` |
2151	
2152	The organizers may add providers; `llm_providers` lists them all, the models the platform hosts itself included,
2153	each under its own id with its base URL in `<MODEL>_BASE_URL`. Any path under a provider's base works
2154	(messages, chat completions, responses, embeddings, model listings) with the request's method and body intact.
2155	
2156	### Your key
2157	
2158	Send your provider key the way the provider expects it: `x-api-key` (Anthropic), `Authorization: Bearer`
2159	(OpenAI and compatible providers), `x-goog-api-key` or `?key=` (Gemini), or `api-key`. The proxy forwards it
2160	unchanged and never stores, logs or returns it. For test and scored runs, keep it as a [team secret](#team-secrets),
2161	not in your package: we store packages and the review agent reads them.
2162	
2163	With the base-URL variables set, the providers' SDKs need no changes: OpenAI's reads `OPENAI_BASE_URL` and sends
2164	`OPENAI_API_KEY` as `Authorization: Bearer`, Anthropic's reads `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` and sends `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`
2165	as `x-api-key`:
2166	
2167	```python
2168	from openai import OpenAI
2169	
2170	client = OpenAI()  # reads OPENAI_BASE_URL and OPENAI_API_KEY
2171	```
2172	
2173	A client that cannot set the provider's own header may send the key as `x-provider-key`; the proxy forwards it in
2174	the provider's header. For Google's Gemini SDK, set the HTTP base URL explicitly:
2175	
2176	```python
2177	import os
2178	from google import genai
2179	
2180	client = genai.Client(api_key=os.environ["GEMINI_API_KEY"],
2181	    http_options={"base_url": os.environ["LLM_PROXY_URL"] + "/google"})
2182	```
2183	
2184	```javascript
2185	import { GoogleGenAI } from "@google/genai"
2186	
2187	const client = new GoogleGenAI({ apiKey: process.env.GEMINI_API_KEY,
2188	  httpOptions: { baseUrl: process.env.LLM_PROXY_URL + "/google" } })
2189	```
2190	
2191	A request without a key of its own gets `401` "Add your <provider> API key to the request.", unless the
2192	organizers pay for that provider: then the proxy adds their key to a run's calls. In that case a scored run's
2193	key variable for that provider (for example `OPENAI_API_KEY`) holds the run token as a placeholder, so SDKs
2194	start, unless you have a team secret by that name; the proxy never forwards the token.
2195	
2196	**Development outside runs:** with your personal token you may use the proxy without a run, at
2197	`$API/llm/<provider>/…` with the header `x-atira-team-key: <token>`, or at `$API/llm/team/<token>/<provider>/…`
2198	(prefer the header: a token lasts 90 days, and URLs end up in logs). Bring your own key; this usage is recorded
2199	for your team and never ranked. Older clients may still call `$API/llm/<provider>/…` with the run token in
2200	`x-api-key` and the provider key in `x-provider-key`. Without a run token or personal token, the proxy answers
2201	`401`.
2202	
2203	A request body may be up to 32 MiB (`413` above that), enough for several full-screen screenshots and a long
2204	context.
2205	
2206	### How cost is measured
2207	
2208	Every call is recorded. Reported usage, including cached input and thinking tokens, is priced at each
2209	provider's published per-token prices for that model, with any deployment-specific prices published by the organizers.
2210	A model too new for the platform's price list counts at the price OpenRouter lists for it, its long-context price
2211	included. An upstream-reported USD cost takes precedence. OpenRouter reports one for every call (send
2212	`"usage": {"include": true}` with older clients), so models without a published price are accepted there; a call
2213	that reports no cost is charged at the highest published price. Elsewhere, unpriced models and models outside
2214	a configured allowlist are refused before forwarding. Streamed calls count too: the proxy asks OpenAI-compatible
2215	providers for a stream's usage (`stream_options.include_usage`), so a streamed chat completion ends with one more
2216	chunk with empty `choices` and the usage. A stream cut off before its usage, or one whose provider reports none, counts
2217	an estimate from the text that arrived and from the request, about four characters per token; a client that hangs up
2218	early is still billed for everything the provider sends. There is no spending limit. Model listings and other
2219	endpoints without inference usage cost nothing; Anthropic `count_tokens` also costs nothing. All network and
2220	fair-play rules still apply, including when using provider-side tools.
2221	
2222	The models the platform hosts itself (`GET /v1/models/status` lists them with their prices) are free to use, never
2223	charged; each call counts toward your run's cost at simulated API prices, so the cost ranking stays honest.
2224	
2225	### Team secrets
2226	
2227	Team secrets are environment variables for your agent's run step in test runs and scored runs, such as
2228	`OPENAI_API_KEY`. Manage them on the team page under Secrets, or with your personal token:
2229	
2230	```sh
2231	curl -X PUT -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" -H "content-type: application/json" \
2232	  --data '{"value": "sk-…"}' "$API/v1/teams/me/secrets/OPENAI_API_KEY"
2233	curl -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" "$API/v1/teams/me/secrets"   # names and dates only
2234	curl -X DELETE -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" "$API/v1/teams/me/secrets/OPENAI_API_KEY"
2235	```
2236	
2237	Values are encrypted, never shown again and redacted from run logs; saving a name again replaces its value.
2238	Setup never receives them. Names are uppercase letters, digits and underscores, starting with a letter, and
2239	cannot be platform variables (`CHALLENGE_*`, `*_BASE_URL`, `*_SERVER_URL`, `*_PROXY`, `LLM_PROXY_URL`,
2240	`CDP_URL`, `CDP_URLS`, `BROWSER_COUNT`, `PATH`, `HOME`, `DISPLAY`, …). A team keeps at most 20; each value is 16 characters to 4 KB long.
2241	
2242	## Scored run
2243	
2244	Each scored submission runs once in the sandbox on the public dataset (RFQ's `public-1`) and is scored; that run
2245	ranks on the leaderboard. The final run at the end of the hackathon uses the same sandbox on a private dataset (see
2246	[Submitting](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/submitting.md#what-happens-next)). Runs are created from your uploaded package. The sandbox is
2247	a Linux VM with a desktop at 1280×800, a **headful Chromium** already open with the Chrome DevTools Protocol on
2248	`127.0.0.1:9222` (or up to four, see [Browsers](#browsers)) and these toolchains, ready for your user:
2249	
2250	- **TypeScript and JavaScript:** Node 24 (runs `.ts` files directly), npm, pnpm and bun.
2251	- **Python:** Python 3.12 and uv (`uv venv`, `uv pip install`, `uv run`); there is no system pip.
2252	- **Rust:** stable Rust (1.99) with cargo. Fetch crates during setup; the run is offline except for the platform
2253	  and the websites.
2254	- gcc, make, git, curl and jq.
2255	
2256	1. **Setup (not counted toward your time, up to 5 minutes):** your `setup` command runs with network access but without any credentials, e.g. to install dependencies.
2257	2. **Model warm-up (not counted toward your time):** the models the platform hosts itself, when it offers any, scale
2258	   to zero when nobody uses them, and waking one takes one to eight minutes. The platform wakes them as soon as your
2259	   run leaves the queue and starts your run only once they're warm (at most 10 minutes after setup), so a cold start
2260	   never counts toward your time. The run's log says when they're warm. While runs are active, the platform keeps
2261	   them warm. `"models"` in `agent.json` lists the ones your agent system calls, by their `provider` id from
2262	   `GET /v1/models/status` (the start page shows it too); the run waits for those alone, and `"models": []` starts it
2263	   right after setup:
2264	
2265	   ```json
2266	   {"setup": ["uv", "sync"], "run": ["uv", "run", "python", "agent.py"], "models": []}
2267	   ```
2268	
2269	   Without it the run waits for every hosted model. Anything else, such as an unknown id, rejects the package with
2270	   `Invalid agent.json: models: …` and the ids it takes. It decides only the wait: your run may call any hosted model
2271	   whatever it lists, but one it didn't list may still be waking.
2272	
2273	   **If a hosted model fails mid-run:** retry failed calls, as with any provider; a short outage is yours to ride out.
2274	   If our models were down for most of the run (from the first failed call on, a 5xx from our model or a lost
2275	   connection to it, at least 8 in 10 of the run's hosted-model calls failed, over at least half its time) and the run
2276	   then ended without an answer, the platform failed, not your agent system: the run doesn't count toward ranking or
2277	   any limit, and a scored run starts again once by itself. A
2278	   run that answered keeps its result.
2279	3. **Run (timed):** your `run` command starts with this environment. The clock starts here.
2280	
2281	| Variable | Value |
2282	| --- | --- |
2283	| `CHALLENGE_API_URL` | the API; read your task at `$CHALLENGE_API_URL/v1/runs/current` |
2284	| `CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN` | the run token |
2285	| `CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS` | the websites with this run's logins, as JSON: the same as `access` |
2286	| `LLM_PROXY_URL` | `$CHALLENGE_API_URL/llm/run/$CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN` |
2287	| `<MODEL>_BASE_URL`, `<MODEL>_API_KEY` | for each model the platform hosts (`GET /v1/models/status`; the start page names them): its base URL through the proxy, under `$LLM_PROXY_URL/<provider>`, and the run token as its key |
2288	| `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/anthropic` |
2289	| `OPENAI_BASE_URL` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/openai/v1` |
2290	| `GOOGLE_GEMINI_BASE_URL` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/google`; set the Gemini SDK's HTTP base URL explicitly as above |
2291	| `MISTRAL_SERVER_URL`, `TOGETHER_BASE_URL` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/mistral`, `$LLM_PROXY_URL/together/v1` |
2292	| your [team secrets](#team-secrets) | for example `OPENAI_API_KEY` with your own key |
2293	| `CDP_URL` | `http://127.0.0.1:9222`, browser 1 |
2294	| `CDP_URLS` | every browser's CDP URL in order, as a JSON array: `["http://127.0.0.1:9222"]` for one browser |
2295	| `BROWSER_COUNT` | how many browsers the sandbox started: `1` unless `agent.json` asks for more |
2296	| `DISPLAY` | `:1`, browser 1's screen; browser n is on `:n` |
2297	| `HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY` (and lowercase) | `http://127.0.0.1:3128`, the only way out of the sandbox |
2298	| `NO_PROXY` | `localhost,127.0.0.1` (CDP stays local) |
2299	
2300	The platform sets no API key variables of its own, except the run-token placeholder for a provider the
2301	organizers pay for (above). `setup` runs first, with network (install your dependencies there) but without the
2302	run's variables or your team secrets, and nothing it starts survives into the run. The run itself reaches only our API and the challenge's websites,
2303	through that proxy; Chromium is already configured to use it. A scored run of RFQ has 20 minutes; a run that
2304	ends without an answer scores 0.

2306	## Browsers
2307	
2308	The sandbox starts one browser unless `agent.json` asks for more, up to four:
2309	
2310	```json
2311	{"setup": ["uv", "sync"], "run": ["uv", "run", "python", "agent.py"], "browsers": 3}
2312	```
2313	
2314	`browsers` is a whole number from 1 to 4; anything else rejects the package with
2315	`Invalid agent.json: browsers: must be a whole number from 1 to 4`. Browser n is its own headful Chromium with its
2316	own profile, on display `:n` (1280×800) with the Chrome DevTools Protocol on port 9221 + n (9222 to 9225), behind
2317	the same proxy as browser 1. All of them are ready before the clock starts. `CDP_URL` stays browser 1, `CDP_URLS` lists all of
2318	them in order, and `BROWSER_COUNT` says how many there are. With three:
2319	
2320	| Variable | Value |
2321	| --- | --- |
2322	| `CDP_URL` | `http://127.0.0.1:9222` |
2323	| `CDP_URLS` | `["http://127.0.0.1:9222","http://127.0.0.1:9223","http://127.0.0.1:9224"]` |
2324	| `BROWSER_COUNT` | `3` |
2325	
2326	**At most 4 browsers run at a time:** ask for up to 4 in `agent.json` (`"browsers"`), use tabs and browser contexts
2327	inside them freely, and don't start browsers of your own, headless ones included. The scored sandbox enforces it:
2328	any other browser the agent starts is stopped within seconds, and the run's logs say so with
2329	`[platform] stopped a browser the agent started: at most 4 run at a time; use the browsers from CDP_URLS`. Every
2330	browser then is one the platform can show and record: test runs show them side by side while they run, with a
2331	recording of each afterwards.
2332	
2333	On your own machine, developing with the scouting logins, `CDP_URLS` is not set and your agent starts its own
2334	browsers.

2340	# Building your agent
2341	
2342	Your agent system has to be agentic: a model decides where to go on the websites, finds the information and makes
2343	the decisions, at run time. How is up to you: drive the browser through the DOM, through pixels, or both; use one
2344	model or several, in parallel if you like; give the model tools and helpers for the browser, parsing, arithmetic and
2345	checks. The model chooses where to go, what to search for and which documents matter. Rejected in review: a fixed
2346	script that clicks through known pages with the model unused or only as a fallback, and a crawler that collects the
2347	websites and hands everything to the model at the end.
2348	
2349	## The browser
2350	
2351	In the sandbox a headful Chromium runs on the desktop (`DISPLAY=:1`, 1280×800) with CDP on
2352	`127.0.0.1:9222`.
2353	
2354	- **DOM agents:** attach with Playwright (`chromium.connect_over_cdp(CDP_URL)`) or any CDP client.
2355	- **Pixel agents:** take screenshots and send mouse and keyboard input to the desktop (`xdotool` and
2356	  ImageMagick's `import` are installed), for example to drive Claude's computer-use tool.
2357	- **Locally:** without `CDP_URL`, launch your own Chromium. The websites are the same: `eval "$(atira scout --env)"`
2358	  gives your agent the scouting logins in `CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS`, the way a run gets its logins.
2359	
2360	### Several browsers
2361	
2362	To work on several websites at once, ask for up to four browsers in `agent.json`:
2363	
2364	```json
2365	{"setup": ["npm", "ci"], "run": ["node", "agent.js"], "browsers": 2}
2366	```
2367	
2368	Each is its own Chromium on its own screen (browser n on `DISPLAY=:n`), and `CDP_URLS` lists their CDP URLs in
2369	order (`CDP_URL` stays the first). With Playwright:
2370	
2371	```javascript
2372	import { chromium } from "playwright"
2373	
2374	const sites = JSON.parse(process.env.CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS)
2375	const browsers = await Promise.all(JSON.parse(process.env.CDP_URLS).map((url) => chromium.connectOverCDP(url)))
2376	const pages = browsers.map((browser) => browser.contexts()[0].pages()[0])
2377	await Promise.all([pages[0].goto(sites[0].url), pages[1].goto(sites[1].url)])
2378	```
2379	
2380	At most 4 browsers run at a time. Use tabs (`context.newPage()`) and browser contexts (`browser.newContext()`)
2381	inside them as freely as you like, but don't start browsers of your own, headless ones included: the sandbox stops
2382	them and says so in the run's logs. A test run shows its browsers side by side while it runs and keeps a recording
2383	of each. Locally there is no `CDP_URLS`: on your machine your agent starts its own browsers.
2384	
2385	## Models
2386	
2387	The hosted models are free to use. Every run gets `QWEN_BASE_URL` and `QWEN_API_KEY` for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, an
2388	OpenAI-compatible chat model with tool calls and images; on your machine `atira scout --env` sets the same variables,
2389	pointed at `atira models proxy`. You can also bring your own key for any provider through the metering proxy;
2390	[how cost is measured](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#how-cost-is-measured) has the details. After quality you are ranked on cost × time, so a cheaper model or a faster run that gets the answer right moves you
2391	up.
2392	
2393	## What makes it hard, on purpose
2394	
2395	The websites are designed to trip agents up: cookie walls, flaky error pages that need a retry, expiring sessions
2396	that send you back to the login, documents inside iframes and ZIP files, popups that close themselves, paging and
2397	"load more" buttons, look-alike records, superseded versions shown first, a timezone that is not yours. Treat
2398	every page as adversarial and verify what you read.
2399	
2400	## Tips
2401	
2402	- Read the brief's rules carefully: they define the one correct answer.
2403	- Keep what the model reads small: page text without duplicated labels, only the parts you need.
2404	- Use prompt caching for your system prompt and tool definitions.
2405	- Re-read a page after every action that changes it; pages update asynchronously.
2406	- Drive four browsers in parallel, one per website (`"browsers": 4`, see [Several browsers](#several-browsers)):
2407	  reading the four sites at once speeds up each run and your iteration, at the cost of more complex code.
2408	- Validate your answer against `answer_schema` before sending it; a `400` costs only time.
2409	- Submit before the clock runs out: a scored run has 20 minutes (`expires_at` in the run). Every part of the answer
2410	  scores on its own, so have your agent submit its best answer about a minute before the end rather than keep
2411	  searching; a run that ends without an answer scores 0.
2412	- Develop against the public websites locally (`atira scout --env`), then test in the sandbox (`atira test-run`):
2413	  a test run shows the full score breakdown, so use it to find what your agent gets wrong.
2414	- Work the answer out from the websites: the final run, which weighs most for the winners, uses a private dataset that is similar, not the same. It has the same jobs (a tender portal, a supplier portal, an ERP and a webmail inbox), the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different software, with a different look, navigation and site names, other content and data, and the information split differently across them. Your agent has to handle it as it finds it.
2415	
2416	## Starter kit
2417	
2418	[`starter-kit/`](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/starter-kit.tar.gz) is a minimal Python skeleton, not an agent: it reads the run and
2419	submits an answer, attaches to the run's browsers over CDP with Playwright, and shows one call to each hosted model.
2420	Your agent goes in `solve()` in `agent.py`; out of the box it exits without an answer. Start from it or from scratch.

2426	# Fair play
2427	
2428	**Rules at a glance**
2429	
2430	You submit an agentic system: one agent or several. In the sandbox it does the whole job on its own: finds what it needs on the four websites, works out the bid and submits it. Nobody helps it during a run.
2431	
2432	**Not allowed**
2433	
2434	- **Hardcoding:** copying values from the websites into your package (prices, material numbers, totals, discounts, logins, TANs), including in prompts and notes, also as defaults or fallbacks. Using what the task brief tells every team, like the sales director's mailbox, is fine.
2435	- **Pre-solving:** working out the answer yourself, or having an AI assistant do it, and putting the result in your package. Exploring the sites with an assistant is fine.
2436	- **Scripts instead of agents:** a fixed click path, or a crawler that grabs everything for one model call. A model has to choose where to go, what to search for and what matters.
2437	- **Outside help during a run:** contacting anything besides our platform and the four websites, calling a model other than through our proxy (your own API keys work through it), running a model inside the sandbox, or starting your own browsers (use the up to 4 provided). Setup may install dependencies.
2438	
2439	**How it's checked:** an AI reviewer reads every submitted package before its scored run. Unclear cases are flagged and stay off the leaderboard until an organizer has looked. The final runs on websites and data your system hasn't seen.
2440	
2441	The details follow.
2442	
2443	## Allowed
2444	
2445	- Any agent design; the free hosted models, or any provider and model with your own key, through the proxy; any
2446	  amount of tokens.
2447	  The proxy forwards your calls unchanged and measures them: reported usage is metered at the published model
2448	  prices, and an upstream-reported USD cost takes precedence. See [the run contract](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#llm-calls)
2449	  for SDK configuration.
2450	- Keeping your model key as a [team secret](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#team-secrets) rather than in your package.
2451	- Your own code, prompts and tools; open-source libraries installed during setup.
2452	- Using what you learned with the scouting logins and in test runs about how the websites work.
2453	- Up to 4 browsers at a time: ask for them with `"browsers"` in `agent.json` and use as many tabs and browser
2454	  contexts inside them as you like.
2455	
2456	## Not allowed
2457	
2458	- Hardcoding values copied from the public scenario or its websites into code, config, prompts or notes, including defaults and fallbacks: tender references, material numbers, prices, totals, discounts, logins and TANs. Facts the task brief states for every scenario, such as the sales director's mailbox, are
2459	  rules you may use.
2460	- A scripted solution. Your agent system must be agentic: a model decides where to go on the websites, finds the
2461	  information and makes the decisions. Code can help it (browser control, parsing, arithmetic, checks, reading a
2462	  page or document the model chose, paging through results it asked for), and several agents and browsers may work
2463	  in parallel. Rejected: a fixed script that clicks through known pages with the model unused or only as a fallback,
2464	  and a crawler that collects the websites and hands everything to the model at the end.
2465	- Bundling or running a local model, or reaching any model other than through the proxy.
2466	- Contacting hosts other than the API and the challenge's websites, or trying to get data out of the sandbox.
2467	- Starting browsers of your own in the sandbox, headless ones included. At most 4 browsers run at a time: ask for up
2468	  to 4 in `agent.json` (`"browsers"`), use tabs and browser contexts inside them freely, and don't start others.
2469	  On your own machine (developing with the scouting logins) your agent starts its own browsers; that is up to you.
2470	- Attacking the platform, the websites, the sandbox or other teams; sharing scored-run data.
2471	
2472	## How it is checked
2473	
2474	- **Package review before any scored run:** an AI code reviewer, a coding agent that reads your whole package in an
2475	  isolated VM. Outcomes: passed, flagged or rejected (no runs). A flagged package still runs and scores, but its
2476	  result stays off the public leaderboard and the activity feed until an organizer passes it; your team sees it
2477	  marked "flagged: waiting for an organizer". Notes and docs addressed to the reviewer are not evidence of compliance
2478	  and do not count against you on their own. Instructions trying to steer the reviewer's verdict do.
2479	  The reviewer's reasons stay with the organizers: your team reads "Flagged by the reviewing agent" or "Rejected by
2480	  the reviewing agent". Someone from Atira looks at flagged packages shortly and unflags a misdetection; if you think
2481	  a reject is one, contact the Atira team.
2482	- **The organizers decide flagged packages, and can look at any submission:** they pass it, add an internal note
2483	  (this changes nothing you or the leaderboard see) or disqualify it. A disqualified submission and its runs read
2484	  "disqualified": it leaves the leaderboard and the final run, its runs still going stop, and your team page shows the
2485	  organizers' reason.
2486	- **Hardcoded values:** the reviewer rejects copied scenario values in code or config, even in defaults or fallbacks.
2487	- **The final run** uses a private dataset that is similar, not the same. It has the same jobs (a tender portal, a
2488	  supplier portal, an ERP and a webmail inbox), the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different software,
2489	  with a different look, navigation and site names, other content and data, and the information split differently
2490	  across them. Your agent has to handle it as it finds it. That run weighs most when we pick the
2491	  winners, so build a system that works the answer out from the websites, not one tuned to the public scenario.
2492	- **The sandbox** reaches only our API and the websites, so every model call passes the proxy and is measured.
2493	  Your team secrets reach only the timed run step and are redacted from its logs.
2494	- **Website logins** exist only for a live run and stop working when it ends.
2495	- **Browsers:** the sandbox stops any browser your agent starts beyond the ones it asked for and notes it in the
2496	  run's logs: `[platform] stopped a browser the agent started`.
2497	- **Everything measured** (tokens, cost, time, the answer) is recorded by the platform, never reported by you.
2498	
2499	Breaking these rules gets the submission rejected before it runs, or removed later; repeated or deliberate attempts
2500	get the team disqualified.

2502	## Flagged results
2503	
2504	A flagged result stays off the public leaderboard until an organizer passes it. **Show flagged** on the leaderboard
2505	lists flagged results, without a rank.

2511	# Submitting
2512	
2513	> In this document, `$API` is https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai (the CLI and API guide call it `$ATIRA_API`).
2514	
2515	You submit your agent system as a gzipped tarball. We review it, run it once in the sandbox on the public dataset
2516	and score it. That run determines its rank on the leaderboard. When the hackathon ends, your latest submission that
2517	passed review runs once more, on a private dataset, in the [final run](#what-happens-next), which weighs most when we pick the winners.
2518	
2519	## Package layout
2520	
2521	```
2522	agent.json          {"setup": ["uv", "sync"], "run": ["uv", "run", "python", "agent.py"], "models": ["qwen"]}
2523	pyproject.toml      (or package.json, requirements.txt, ...)
2524	agent.py            your code
2525	```
2526	
2527	- `agent.json` at the root: `setup` (optional) and `run`, each an argv array. Both run in the package directory.
2528	  `browsers` (optional, 1 to 4, default 1) is how many browsers the sandbox starts for the run; see
2529	  [the run contract](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#browsers). `models` (optional) lists the hosted models your agent system calls,
2530	  by provider id, all of them by default: the run's clock waits for those to warm up, and `[]` starts it right after
2531	  setup; see [the run contract](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#scored-run).
2532	- At most 20 MB compressed; regular files only.
2533	- No secrets: the run gets everything it needs from the environment.
2534	
2535	## Upload
2536	
2537	```
2538	tar czf agent.tar.gz -C my-agent .
2539	curl --data-binary @agent.tar.gz \
2540	  -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" -H "content-type: application/gzip" \
2541	  $API/v1/challenges/rfq/submissions
2542	```
2543	
2544	The response (`202`) has your submission's id. Review is still pending and no runs exist yet: follow it with
2545	`GET $API/v1/challenges/rfq/submissions` for the review result and run ids, or watch the leaderboard.
2546	
2547	`$ATIRA_TOKEN` is your personal token: `atira login` signs the [CLI](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/cli.md) in through the browser, and
2548	`atira token` prints the token (or sign in with plain curl, as the [API guide](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/api.md#signing-in) shows).
2549	
2550	Or let the CLI pack, check and upload the folder: `atira submit my-agent` (and `atira test-run my-agent` for a
2551	test run). It leaves out `.git`, `node_modules` and what `.gitignore` excludes. In a terminal, `submit` then opens
2552	your team page, which shows the review and links each scored run as it starts, and `test-run` opens the run page.
2553	
2554	## Test it in the sandbox first
2555	
2556	Upload the same tarball as a test run ("Test runs" on your team page, or
2557	`POST $API/v1/challenges/rfq/rehearsals` with the same headers). It runs once in the scored-run sandbox against
2558	the public scenario `public-1`, scored with the points for each part of the answer. Its live view shows the
2559	browser (a frame about every 1.5 s, or the live screen where available), the phases, every model call,
2560	and your logs as the agent prints them. Afterwards the recorded video stays available to
2561	your team. Up to 5 test runs at a time per team. `atira test-run my-agent` uploads it, starts the run
2562	and opens it live; `atira cancel` (or Cancel run on the run page) stops a run that has not finished, and frees its
2563	test-run slot at once.
2564	
2565	## Linking your GitHub repository
2566	
2567	The organizers ask each team to link the GitHub repository it builds its agent in, so they can review the
2568	code, for example to compare a winning submission with its source. On your team page, the captain chooses
2569	Connect a GitHub repository, installs the organizers' GitHub App on the account that owns the repository
2570	(granting it only that repository is enough), and picks the repository. Every member sees the linked repository,
2571	who linked it and when; the captain can switch or unlink it at any time.
2572	
2573	The app only reads the contents of the repositories you grant it; it cannot push, open issues or change
2574	settings. Linking does not change how you submit: scored submissions and test runs are still the tarballs
2575	described above. To withdraw access completely, unlink the repository and uninstall the app in your GitHub
2576	settings.
2577	
2578	## Watching your submission
2579	
2580	Each scored run has a live view with its phase, timer, model calls, tokens and cost. On the public dataset it also
2581	shows your team the browser (frames, and the live screen where available), the logs and errors
2582	unredacted and the scenario id, and the recording afterwards. The final run on the private dataset shows its
2583	screen, frames and recordings to the organizers only; your team reads its logs and errors with private values
2584	masked as `[private]`.
2585	
2586	## Resubmitting
2587	
2588	Submit as often as you like, one at a time: while a submission is still in review or has unfinished runs, the
2589	next upload is refused with `429`. Your **best complete** submission holds your place on the leaderboard; your
2590	**latest** one that passed review goes into the final run. Your other submissions stay in your history at
2591	`$API/team`. Cancelling a submission's scored run ends that submission: it never completes, the leaderboard ignores it, and you
2592	can submit again.
2593	
2594	## What happens next
2595	
2596	1. **Review:** passed, flagged or rejected (no runs). A flagged submission still runs and scores, but its result
2597	   stays off the public leaderboard and the activity feed until an organizer passes it; your team sees it marked
2598	   "flagged: waiting for an organizer". Your team sees the outcome, not the reviewer's reasons. The organizers can
2599	   still pass or disqualify a submission later; a disqualified one reads "disqualified", leaves the leaderboard and
2600	   the final run, and your team page gives the organizers' reason.
2601	2. **Scored run:** one run in a fresh sandbox on the public dataset, setup first (up to 5 minutes, not counted),
2602	   then your run command (timed).
2603	3. **Ranking:** once the run has finished and review is passed, your submission appears on the leaderboard with its quality, cost and
2604	   time; ineligible answers rank after every eligible one.
2605	4. **Final run:** when the hackathon ends, the organizers run every team's latest submission that passed review
2606	   (organizers resolve outstanding reviewer flags before the final run starts; rejected and disqualified ones don't count) once by default (or best of three if you opt in before the final run starts) on a private dataset that is similar, not the same. It has the same jobs (a tender portal, a supplier portal, an ERP and a webmail inbox), the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different software, with a different look, navigation and site names, other content and data, and the information split differently across them. Your agent has to handle it as it finds it. It is the latest one, not the best one.
2607	   That run weighs most when we pick the winners ([Winners](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/scoring.md#winners)), so build a system that works the answer out from the websites, not one tuned to
2608	   the public scenario. Its results stay with the organizers until they publish them; then the leaderboard shows
2609	   the final results, tagged "Private dataset · final", and the public-dataset board stays at
2610	   `$API/challenges/rfq/leaderboard?dataset=public`.
2611	
2612	## Final private evaluation: one attempt or best of three
2613	
2614	The final runs your latest passed submission once, or up to three times if you opt in to **Best of 3** on your team
2615	page before the final starts (`atira final --best-of 3`). Your best attempt counts. Details:
2616	[Answers and scoring](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/scoring.md#final-private-evaluation-one-attempt-or-best-of-three).

2643	## FAQ
2644	
2645	**Which models can I use?** The hosted models are free, and the starter kit shows how to call them. Or bring your own key for

2648	price (a model too new for the platform's list counts at the price OpenRouter lists for it; OpenRouter reports its own)
2649	and satisfy any organizer model allowlist. See
2650	[the run contract](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#llm-calls) for SDK setup.
2651	
2652	**Where do I keep my model key?** As a [team secret](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#team-secrets): the team page's Secrets list
2653	injects it into your agent's run step in test and scored runs, redacted from logs. Don't put keys in your
2654	package; we store packages and the review agent reads them.
2655	
2656	**Why does my model call get a 401?** "Add your OpenAI API key to the request" means no provider key arrived: set
2657	`OPENAI_API_KEY` (in test and scored runs, as a [team secret](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#team-secrets)). A 401 from the
2658	provider itself means the key is wrong. Check that `OPENAI_BASE_URL` points at the run's proxy
2659	(`$LLM_PROXY_URL/openai/v1`, already set in test and scored runs); the same holds for any OpenAI-compatible provider.
2660	
2661	**How do my teammates and I sign in from a terminal?** Each person runs `atira login` on their own computer
2662	and approves it in the browser. Every device gets its own token; there is no shared team key to pass around.
2663	Without a browser on the machine, `atira login --device` prints a link and a code to approve elsewhere.
2664	
2665	**I lost a laptop, or a token leaked.** Revoke that device's token on your team page under Signed-in devices
2666	(`atira logout` revokes the one on the computer you are at). Leaving or being removed from a team ends your
2667	tokens' access to it at once.
2668	
2669	**My invite link says it is for someone else.** Invites are for one GitHub account. Sign in with the account
2670	the captain invited, or ask the captain to invite your GitHub username.
2671	
2672	**Does it cost me anything?** We charge nothing, and the models the platform hosts are free and never charged. If
2673	you bring your own key for another provider, that provider bills your key. The proxy measures every call and
2674	ranks you on its cost at the published prices; hosted calls count at simulated API prices.
2675	
2676	**How can I try my agent?** Develop locally against the public websites (`atira scout --env` exports the
2677	scouting logins), then test in the sandbox (`atira test-run ./my-agent`). A test run runs on `public-1`, the public
2678	RFQ scenario, and returns your score with the points for each part of the answer. With the scouting logins nothing
2679	counts: a bid entered on the tender portal is acknowledged without counting.
2680	
2681	**Is the public scenario's answer published?** No. The correct answer isn't published; your system has to work it
2682	out from the websites. Score breakdowns show the points for each part of the answer, never the expected values.
2683	
2684	**Which submission counts?** Your best submission holds your place on the leaderboard, which ranks scored runs on
2685	the public dataset. Your latest one that passed review (not your best one) goes into the final run: when the
2686	hackathon ends, the organizers run it once by default (or best of three if you opt in before the final run starts) on a private dataset that is similar, not the same. It has the same jobs (a tender portal, a supplier portal, an ERP and a webmail inbox), the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different software, with a different look, navigation and site names, other content and data, and the information split differently across them. Your agent has to handle it as it finds it.
2687	That run weighs most when we pick the winners, ahead of your public score and the elegance of your system, so
2688	build an agent that works the answer out from the websites, not one tuned to the public scenario. See
2689	[Winners](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/scoring.md#winners).
2690	
2691	**Why did my answer get a 400?** It does not match `answer_schema`. The response lists the issues; the run is
2692	still open, so fix it and send it again.
2693	
2694	**Can I run my agent outside the sandbox?** While you develop, yes, anywhere, with the scouting logins. Test runs
2695	and scored runs always run in our sandbox.
2696	
2697	**Why is my run still queued?** Runs share the sandboxes in a fair order: scored runs first, then teams take turns,
2698	the team with the fewest runs in flight first. Your team runs up to 5 test runs at a time and can have up to 3
2699	waiting; the next waits while other teams' runs start. The run page says how many runs are ahead of yours, and
2700	`atira test-run --follow` prints it. See [the run queue](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/api.md#the-run-queue).
2701	
2702	**How do I stop a run?** `atira cancel <run>`, or Cancel run on its run page. The sandbox is removed, the run fails
2703	with "Cancelled by @you", and you can start the next test run at once. A cancelled scored run ends its
2704	submission: the leaderboard ignores it, and you can submit again.
2705	
2706	**Why do my requests get a 403 "Error 1010"?** The edge in front of our hosts refuses some default HTTP
2707	clients, such as Python's `urllib`. Send your own `User-Agent` header (the starter kit does).
2708	
2709	**Python says `CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED` on my Mac.** Python from python.org ships without CA certificates.
2710	Run `Install Certificates.command` from its folder in Applications, or set `SSL_CERT_FILE=/etc/ssl/cert.pem`.
2711	
2712	**What can my agent reach during a scored run?** Our API (including the model proxy) and the challenge's
2713	websites, nothing else. The `HTTP(S)_PROXY` variables in the run's environment route there; Python's
2714	`urllib`, `requests`, `httpx`, the Anthropic SDK and Node's `fetch` pick them up automatically. Chromium is
2715	already configured. Setup (`uv sync`, `npm ci`, …) has network, but nothing it starts survives into the
2716	run.
2717	
2718	## Event details
2719	
2720	- The event is on 10 October 2026.
2721	- A team has up to five people.
2722	- A scored run has 20 minutes on the clock; a test run has up to 2 hours.
2723	- Ask the organizers about the submission deadline and prizes.
2724	
2725	## Final private evaluation: one attempt or best of three
2726	
2727	The final runs your latest passed submission once, or up to three times if you opt in to **Best of 3** on your team
2728	page before the final starts (`atira final --best-of 3`). Your best attempt counts. Details:
2729	[Answers and scoring](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/scoring.md#final-private-evaluation-one-attempt-or-best-of-three).
2730	
2731	---

# Answers and scoring

> In this document, `$API` is https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai (the CLI and API guide call it `$ATIRA_API`).

Each challenge defines its answer format and how quality is scored; the platform measures cost and time and
ranks everyone the same way. Test runs, scored submissions and the scouting logins use the public dataset (the
websites as you see them, with scenario `public-1`), and the leaderboard ranks those results. The correct answer
isn't published; your system has to work it out from the websites. When the hackathon ends, a [final run](#final-run)
on a private dataset weighs most when we pick the [winners](#winners).

## Per run

- **Quality** (0 to 100): how right the answer is, by the challenge's scorer.
- **Eligible:** whether the answer meets the challenge's mandatory criteria. For RFQ: the right tender reference;
  a wrong decision (bid or no_bid) costs quality points instead.
- **Cost:** the run's LLM usage, priced per model, in USD.
- **Time:** from the start of your run command to your accepted answer.

A malformed answer is rejected with a `400` and does not end the run. A well-formed answer is final, even if it
is wrong. A run without an answer scores quality 0 and is not eligible.

## Leaderboard

Each scored submission runs once in the sandbox on the public dataset and is scored; one run per submission
keeps your model bill down. A submission appears once its run has finished and review is passed; reviewer flags await organizer approval. Each team is ranked by its best
complete submission. The API reports them in its `median_*` fields; with one run per submission, that is
the run's own value.

1. Eligible before ineligible.
2. Higher quality.
3. Lower cost × time: the submission's cost in USD times its time, with cost counted as at least $0.01 and time
   as at least 1 second. Cost and time weigh the same: halving your model bill counts as much as halving your run
   time, and among free runs the faster one wins.
4. The submission ID, when everything above is equal.

On the leaderboard's plot, each team is a dot, quality against cost or time; the dotted line is the Pareto front,
the teams no other eligible team beats on both.

Test runs and scored runs on the public scenario `public-1` show your team the points for each part of the answer,
never the expected values. Runs on the private dataset show quality, eligibility, cost and time without a breakdown.

## Final run

When the hackathon ends, the organizers run every team's latest submission that passed review (organizers resolve outstanding reviewer flags before the final run starts; rejected ones don't count) once by default (or best of three if you opt in before the final run starts) on a private dataset that is similar, not the same. It has the same jobs (a tender portal, a supplier portal, an ERP and a webmail inbox), the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different software, with a different look, navigation and site names, other content and data, and the information split differently across them. Your agent has to handle it as it finds it, and each run's brief states the bid rules. It ranks in the same order as above. Build an agent that works the
answer out from the websites, not one tuned to the public scenario.

## Winners

We pick the winners on three things, roughly in this order:

1. Performance on the private dataset (the final run).
2. Performance on the public dataset (the leaderboard).
3. The elegance of the system.

It is the latest submission, not the best one: your best submission holds your place on the leaderboard; your
latest one that passed review goes into the final run. The final run's results stay with the organizers until they
publish them. Then the leaderboard shows the final results, tagged "Private dataset · final", with each team's
public-dataset result and its change in rank beside them, and the public-dataset board stays at `$API/challenges/rfq/leaderboard?dataset=public` (Markdown:
`leaderboard.md?dataset=public`; API: `GET /v1/challenges/rfq/leaderboard?dataset=public`).

## RFQ scoring

The brief states the calculation rules. Each position has four optional fields that earn independent points:
`base_unit_price` (the EUR scale price per piece before discount), `surcharge_per_unit` (material surcharge plus
ordinary and allocated setup cost per piece, before discount), `packaging_per_unit`, and `rebate_total` (the
project-bonus credit for the **entire position**). Leave a field blank if unanswered; enter zero for a known zero.
The same calculation rules and answer format apply to the public and private datasets. You can also explicitly
omit unfinished positions in the form; completed fields retain their credit. You must sign and submit to score.

| Part (a bid) | Points |
| --- | --- |
| Decision | 5 |
| Tender reference | 5 |
| Discount percent | 5 |
| Total net (to the cent, consistent with the positions) | 5 |
| Arithmetic (every position, and a total that is their sum) | 5 |
| Withdrawn Q&A quantity check (when present) | 5 |
| Dated metal-index check (when present) | 5 |
| Positions (split evenly): material 20 %, quantity 15 %, base price 15 %, surcharge 10 %, packaging 10 %, project bonus 10 %, unit price 10 %, lead time 10 % | 75 minus the checks above |


For a no_bid case: decision 75, tender reference 5, no positions 5, a total of 0 15. A wrong decision costs its
points but leaves the other fields their credit.

Money is compared to the cent. Positions are matched by their position number; extra or duplicate positions cost
one position's share each.

## Final private evaluation: one attempt or best of three

The final runs your latest passed submission on the private set. The default is one attempt.
Before the final run starts, opt in to **Best of 3** on your team page or run
`atira final --best-of 3` (`--best-of 1` opts out). `atira status` shows the choice.
When the final run starts, each team's choice is fixed, including teams still in review.
Opted-in teams get up to three attempts on the same private scenario(s). Your **single best complete attempt**
counts: eligible first, then higher quality, then lower cost × time, with the leaderboard's usual floors.
It is not an average, and a failed attempt does not outweigh a better successful one.
Every attempt is kept. Your team sees its own attempts' logs (private values masked) and, once the organizers publish the final, the results.
Calls using your own model keys can cost up to **3×**. The public leaderboard remains one run per submission
on the public scenario. Review, flags and disqualification work as for any submission.

Flagged results are hidden from the public leaderboard by default. **Show flagged** on the page (or `?flagged=1` on
the leaderboard API) lists them beside the approved ones, tagged "flagged: waiting for an organizer" and without a
rank, so showing them does not change other ranks. An organizer pass makes a flagged result count normally.

---

Source: https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md

# How a run works

> In this document, `$API` is https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai (the CLI and API guide call it `$ATIRA_API`).

A run is one attempt at one scenario of one challenge. It starts with a run token, gives your agent a task and
logins for the challenge's websites, and ends when your agent submits its answer or time runs out. Test runs and
scored runs both run your package in the [sandbox](#scored-run); you develop on your own machine with the scouting
logins.

## Develop locally, then test in the sandbox

RFQ has one public scenario, `public-1`: the websites as you see them.

1. **Develop locally** against the public websites with the scouting logins the organizers publish:
   `eval "$(atira scout --env)"` (in PowerShell: `atira scout --env | Out-String | Invoke-Expression`) sets
   `CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS` (the websites and their logins, the JSON a run gets), each website's URL as
   `CHALLENGE_SITE_<ID>_URL`, and `CHALLENGE_SCOUTING`, the `brief`, `access`, `submission` and `answer_schema` of
   `GET $API/v1/challenges/rfq/scouting` as JSON (`CHALLENGE_SCOUTING_URL` is that address). There is no run token.
   Where the platform hosts models, they need no key: `--env` also exports each one's base URL and key, pointed at
   `atira models proxy` on your computer with `local` as the key, so run `atira login` once, then keep
   `atira models proxy` running in another terminal. Those calls are free, recorded and never ranked. Any other
   provider takes your own key.
   Nothing done with these logins counts.
   A bid entered on the tender portal is acknowledged without counting.
2. **Test in the sandbox:** `atira test-run ./my-agent` uploads your package, starts a test run on `public-1` and
   opens its run page live. It runs in the same sandbox as a scored run, but for up to 2 hours instead of 20 minutes (keep it under
   20 to be safe), and the run page shows its
   score with the full breakdown. `atira cancel` stops it early.

## Inside a run

1. **Read the task:** `GET $CHALLENGE_API_URL/v1/runs/current` with the header `x-api-key: $CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN`
   returns:
   - `brief`: the task statement in markdown, with the rules;
   - `access`: one entry per website: `siteId`, `url`, and `credentials` (`username`, `password`);
   - `submission`: where the answer goes: `{"kind": "api", "url": ...}` (POST it to that URL) or
     `{"kind": "site", "siteId": ..., "url": ...}` (submit it on that website, e.g. RFQ's configurator);
   - `answer_url` (API submissions only) and `answer_schema` (JSON Schema of the answer);
   - `started_at`, `expires_at`, and what the run has spent on LLM calls so far.
   - `llm_proxy_url`: the model proxy base with this run's token, `llm_providers` and `llm_base_urls` (each
     provider's proxy base), and `llm_env` (the SDK base-URL variables the run step gets).
   Keep the token secret: it is your agent's identity for this run.
2. **Work:** your agent logs into the websites with those credentials and collects what it needs. Its LLM calls
   go through our metering proxy: a hosted model's with the run token its key variable already holds, any other
   provider's with your own key (below).
3. **Answer** through the run's `submission` target. For an `api` target, `POST` the answer as JSON to
   `answer_url` with the same `x-api-key` header. For a `site` target, submit it on that website: the site
   forwards it to the platform, shows the same validation issues in German, and confirms with a receipt.
   - `400` with `issues`: the answer is malformed. Nothing is recorded, the clock keeps running, fix it and send
     it again.
   - `202`: accepted and final. The run ends, the token and the website logins stop working, and a test run
     returns its score and breakdown. Your agent then has 10 seconds to exit before the platform stops it.

Site logins are issued per run and only work while that run is live. Send tokens in the `x-api-key` header
(`Authorization: Bearer` works too). Send a User-Agent of your own: the edge in
front of the API currently refuses Python's default `Python-urllib/…` agent with 403. Test runs last up to 2 hours.

## LLM calls

Use the [hosted models](#how-cost-is-measured), which are free, or bring your own key for any provider and model.
Every call goes through our proxy, which forwards it unchanged and only measures it: a provider you bring bills your
own key, and the ranking uses what the call costs at the published prices. A scored run's sandbox reaches only our
API and the challenge's websites, so its model calls work only through the proxy; test runs are metered the same way.

The run token sits in the proxy path, so your key keeps its usual header and an SDK needs only a base URL:

```
$API/llm/run/<run token>/<provider>/<the provider's own API path>
```

`llm_proxy_url` is the run's proxy, `<run API>/llm/run/<run token>`; in a test or scored run it is `$LLM_PROXY_URL`. Built-in providers:

| Provider | Forwards to | Base URL for its SDK or an OpenAI-compatible client |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `anthropic` | `https://api.anthropic.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/anthropic` |
| `openai` | `https://api.openai.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/openai/v1` |
| `openrouter` | `https://openrouter.ai/api` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/openrouter/v1` |
| `google` | `https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/google` (Gemini SDK), `…/google/v1beta/openai` |
| `groq` | `https://api.groq.com/openai` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/groq/v1` (use an OpenAI client) |
| `mistral` | `https://api.mistral.ai` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/mistral/v1` |
| `deepseek` | `https://api.deepseek.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/deepseek/v1` |
| `xai` | `https://api.x.ai` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/xai/v1` (HTTP API; the gRPC `xai-sdk` cannot use the proxy) |
| `together` | `https://api.together.xyz` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/together/v1` |
| `fireworks` | `https://api.fireworks.ai/inference` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/fireworks/v1` |

The organizers may add providers; `llm_providers` lists them all, the models the platform hosts itself included,
each under its own id with its base URL in `<MODEL>_BASE_URL`. Any path under a provider's base works
(messages, chat completions, responses, embeddings, model listings) with the request's method and body intact.

### Your key

Send your provider key the way the provider expects it: `x-api-key` (Anthropic), `Authorization: Bearer`
(OpenAI and compatible providers), `x-goog-api-key` or `?key=` (Gemini), or `api-key`. The proxy forwards it
unchanged and never stores, logs or returns it. For test and scored runs, keep it as a [team secret](#team-secrets),
not in your package: we store packages and the review agent reads them.

With the base-URL variables set, the providers' SDKs need no changes: OpenAI's reads `OPENAI_BASE_URL` and sends
`OPENAI_API_KEY` as `Authorization: Bearer`, Anthropic's reads `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` and sends `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`
as `x-api-key`:

```python
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI()  # reads OPENAI_BASE_URL and OPENAI_API_KEY
```

A client that cannot set the provider's own header may send the key as `x-provider-key`; the proxy forwards it in
the provider's header. For Google's Gemini SDK, set the HTTP base URL explicitly:

```python
import os
from google import genai

client = genai.Client(api_key=os.environ["GEMINI_API_KEY"],
    http_options={"base_url": os.environ["LLM_PROXY_URL"] + "/google"})
```

```javascript
import { GoogleGenAI } from "@google/genai"

const client = new GoogleGenAI({ apiKey: process.env.GEMINI_API_KEY,
  httpOptions: { baseUrl: process.env.LLM_PROXY_URL + "/google" } })
```

A request without a key of its own gets `401` "Add your <provider> API key to the request.", unless the
organizers pay for that provider: then the proxy adds their key to a run's calls. In that case a scored run's
key variable for that provider (for example `OPENAI_API_KEY`) holds the run token as a placeholder, so SDKs
start, unless you have a team secret by that name; the proxy never forwards the token.

**Development outside runs:** with your personal token you may use the proxy without a run, at
`$API/llm/<provider>/…` with the header `x-atira-team-key: <token>`, or at `$API/llm/team/<token>/<provider>/…`
(prefer the header: a token lasts 90 days, and URLs end up in logs). Bring your own key; this usage is recorded
for your team and never ranked. Older clients may still call `$API/llm/<provider>/…` with the run token in
`x-api-key` and the provider key in `x-provider-key`. Without a run token or personal token, the proxy answers
`401`.

A request body may be up to 32 MiB (`413` above that), enough for several full-screen screenshots and a long
context.

### How cost is measured

Every call is recorded. Reported usage, including cached input and thinking tokens, is priced at each
provider's published per-token prices for that model, with any deployment-specific prices published by the organizers.
A model too new for the platform's price list counts at the price OpenRouter lists for it, its long-context price
included. An upstream-reported USD cost takes precedence. OpenRouter reports one for every call (send
`"usage": {"include": true}` with older clients), so models without a published price are accepted there; a call
that reports no cost is charged at the highest published price. Elsewhere, unpriced models and models outside
a configured allowlist are refused before forwarding. Streamed calls count too: the proxy asks OpenAI-compatible
providers for a stream's usage (`stream_options.include_usage`), so a streamed chat completion ends with one more
chunk with empty `choices` and the usage. A stream cut off before its usage, or one whose provider reports none, counts
an estimate from the text that arrived and from the request, about four characters per token; a client that hangs up
early is still billed for everything the provider sends. There is no spending limit. Model listings and other
endpoints without inference usage cost nothing; Anthropic `count_tokens` also costs nothing. All network and
fair-play rules still apply, including when using provider-side tools.

The models the platform hosts itself (`GET /v1/models/status` lists them with their prices) are free to use, never
charged; each call counts toward your run's cost at simulated API prices, so the cost ranking stays honest.

### Team secrets

Team secrets are environment variables for your agent's run step in test runs and scored runs, such as
`OPENAI_API_KEY`. Manage them on the team page under Secrets, or with your personal token:

```sh
curl -X PUT -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" -H "content-type: application/json" \
  --data '{"value": "sk-…"}' "$API/v1/teams/me/secrets/OPENAI_API_KEY"
curl -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" "$API/v1/teams/me/secrets"   # names and dates only
curl -X DELETE -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" "$API/v1/teams/me/secrets/OPENAI_API_KEY"
```

Values are encrypted, never shown again and redacted from run logs; saving a name again replaces its value.
Setup never receives them. Names are uppercase letters, digits and underscores, starting with a letter, and
cannot be platform variables (`CHALLENGE_*`, `*_BASE_URL`, `*_SERVER_URL`, `*_PROXY`, `LLM_PROXY_URL`,
`CDP_URL`, `CDP_URLS`, `BROWSER_COUNT`, `PATH`, `HOME`, `DISPLAY`, …). A team keeps at most 20; each value is 16 characters to 4 KB long.

## Scored run

Each scored submission runs once in the sandbox on the public dataset (RFQ's `public-1`) and is scored; that run
ranks on the leaderboard. The final run at the end of the hackathon uses the same sandbox on a private dataset (see
[Submitting](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/submitting.md#what-happens-next)). Runs are created from your uploaded package. The sandbox is
a Linux VM with a desktop at 1280×800, a **headful Chromium** already open with the Chrome DevTools Protocol on
`127.0.0.1:9222` (or up to four, see [Browsers](#browsers)) and these toolchains, ready for your user:

- **TypeScript and JavaScript:** Node 24 (runs `.ts` files directly), npm, pnpm and bun.
- **Python:** Python 3.12 and uv (`uv venv`, `uv pip install`, `uv run`); there is no system pip.
- **Rust:** stable Rust (1.99) with cargo. Fetch crates during setup; the run is offline except for the platform
  and the websites.
- gcc, make, git, curl and jq.

1. **Setup (not counted toward your time, up to 5 minutes):** your `setup` command runs with network access but without any credentials, e.g. to install dependencies.
2. **Model warm-up (not counted toward your time):** the models the platform hosts itself, when it offers any, scale
   to zero when nobody uses them, and waking one takes one to eight minutes. The platform wakes them as soon as your
   run leaves the queue and starts your run only once they're warm (at most 10 minutes after setup), so a cold start
   never counts toward your time. The run's log says when they're warm. While runs are active, the platform keeps
   them warm. `"models"` in `agent.json` lists the ones your agent system calls, by their `provider` id from
   `GET /v1/models/status` (the start page shows it too); the run waits for those alone, and `"models": []` starts it
   right after setup:

   ```json
   {"setup": ["uv", "sync"], "run": ["uv", "run", "python", "agent.py"], "models": []}
   ```

   Without it the run waits for every hosted model. Anything else, such as an unknown id, rejects the package with
   `Invalid agent.json: models: …` and the ids it takes. It decides only the wait: your run may call any hosted model
   whatever it lists, but one it didn't list may still be waking.

   **If a hosted model fails mid-run:** retry failed calls, as with any provider; a short outage is yours to ride out.
   If our models were down for most of the run (from the first failed call on, a 5xx from our model or a lost
   connection to it, at least 8 in 10 of the run's hosted-model calls failed, over at least half its time) and the run
   then ended without an answer, the platform failed, not your agent system: the run doesn't count toward ranking or
   any limit, and a scored run starts again once by itself. A
   run that answered keeps its result.
3. **Run (timed):** your `run` command starts with this environment. The clock starts here.

| Variable | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `CHALLENGE_API_URL` | the API; read your task at `$CHALLENGE_API_URL/v1/runs/current` |
| `CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN` | the run token |
| `CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS` | the websites with this run's logins, as JSON: the same as `access` |
| `LLM_PROXY_URL` | `$CHALLENGE_API_URL/llm/run/$CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN` |
| `<MODEL>_BASE_URL`, `<MODEL>_API_KEY` | for each model the platform hosts (`GET /v1/models/status`; the start page names them): its base URL through the proxy, under `$LLM_PROXY_URL/<provider>`, and the run token as its key |
| `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/anthropic` |
| `OPENAI_BASE_URL` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/openai/v1` |
| `GOOGLE_GEMINI_BASE_URL` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/google`; set the Gemini SDK's HTTP base URL explicitly as above |
| `MISTRAL_SERVER_URL`, `TOGETHER_BASE_URL` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/mistral`, `$LLM_PROXY_URL/together/v1` |
| your [team secrets](#team-secrets) | for example `OPENAI_API_KEY` with your own key |
| `CDP_URL` | `http://127.0.0.1:9222`, browser 1 |
| `CDP_URLS` | every browser's CDP URL in order, as a JSON array: `["http://127.0.0.1:9222"]` for one browser |
| `BROWSER_COUNT` | how many browsers the sandbox started: `1` unless `agent.json` asks for more |
| `DISPLAY` | `:1`, browser 1's screen; browser n is on `:n` |
| `HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY` (and lowercase) | `http://127.0.0.1:3128`, the only way out of the sandbox |
| `NO_PROXY` | `localhost,127.0.0.1` (CDP stays local) |

The platform sets no API key variables of its own, except the run-token placeholder for a provider the
organizers pay for (above). `setup` runs first, with network (install your dependencies there) but without the
run's variables or your team secrets, and nothing it starts survives into the run. The run itself reaches only our API and the challenge's websites,
through that proxy; Chromium is already configured to use it. A scored run of RFQ has 20 minutes; a run that
ends without an answer scores 0.

## Browsers

The sandbox starts one browser unless `agent.json` asks for more, up to four:

```json
{"setup": ["uv", "sync"], "run": ["uv", "run", "python", "agent.py"], "browsers": 3}
```

`browsers` is a whole number from 1 to 4; anything else rejects the package with
`Invalid agent.json: browsers: must be a whole number from 1 to 4`. Browser n is its own headful Chromium with its
own profile, on display `:n` (1280×800) with the Chrome DevTools Protocol on port 9221 + n (9222 to 9225), behind
the same proxy as browser 1. All of them are ready before the clock starts. `CDP_URL` stays browser 1, `CDP_URLS` lists all of
them in order, and `BROWSER_COUNT` says how many there are. With three:

| Variable | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `CDP_URL` | `http://127.0.0.1:9222` |
| `CDP_URLS` | `["http://127.0.0.1:9222","http://127.0.0.1:9223","http://127.0.0.1:9224"]` |
| `BROWSER_COUNT` | `3` |

**At most 4 browsers run at a time:** ask for up to 4 in `agent.json` (`"browsers"`), use tabs and browser contexts
inside them freely, and don't start browsers of your own, headless ones included. The scored sandbox enforces it:
any other browser the agent starts is stopped within seconds, and the run's logs say so with
`[platform] stopped a browser the agent started: at most 4 run at a time; use the browsers from CDP_URLS`. Every
browser then is one the platform can show and record: test runs show them side by side while they run, with a
recording of each afterwards.

On your own machine, developing with the scouting logins, `CDP_URLS` is not set and your agent starts its own
browsers.

# Building your agent

Your agent system has to be agentic: a model decides where to go on the websites, finds the information and makes
the decisions, at run time. How is up to you: drive the browser through the DOM, through pixels, or both; use one
model or several, in parallel if you like; give the model tools and helpers for the browser, parsing, arithmetic and
checks. The model chooses where to go, what to search for and which documents matter. Rejected in review: a fixed
script that clicks through known pages with the model unused or only as a fallback, and a crawler that collects the
websites and hands everything to the model at the end.

## The browser

In the sandbox a headful Chromium runs on the desktop (`DISPLAY=:1`, 1280×800) with CDP on
`127.0.0.1:9222`.

- **DOM agents:** attach with Playwright (`chromium.connect_over_cdp(CDP_URL)`) or any CDP client.
- **Pixel agents:** take screenshots and send mouse and keyboard input to the desktop (`xdotool` and
  ImageMagick's `import` are installed), for example to drive Claude's computer-use tool.
- **Locally:** without `CDP_URL`, launch your own Chromium. The websites are the same: `eval "$(atira scout --env)"`
  gives your agent the scouting logins in `CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS`, the way a run gets its logins.

### Several browsers

To work on several websites at once, ask for up to four browsers in `agent.json`:

```json
{"setup": ["npm", "ci"], "run": ["node", "agent.js"], "browsers": 2}
```

Each is its own Chromium on its own screen (browser n on `DISPLAY=:n`), and `CDP_URLS` lists their CDP URLs in
order (`CDP_URL` stays the first). With Playwright:

```javascript
import { chromium } from "playwright"

const sites = JSON.parse(process.env.CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS)
const browsers = await Promise.all(JSON.parse(process.env.CDP_URLS).map((url) => chromium.connectOverCDP(url)))
const pages = browsers.map((browser) => browser.contexts()[0].pages()[0])
await Promise.all([pages[0].goto(sites[0].url), pages[1].goto(sites[1].url)])
```

At most 4 browsers run at a time. Use tabs (`context.newPage()`) and browser contexts (`browser.newContext()`)
inside them as freely as you like, but don't start browsers of your own, headless ones included: the sandbox stops
them and says so in the run's logs. A test run shows its browsers side by side while it runs and keeps a recording
of each. Locally there is no `CDP_URLS`: on your machine your agent starts its own browsers.

## Models

The hosted models are free to use. Every run gets `QWEN_BASE_URL` and `QWEN_API_KEY` for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, an
OpenAI-compatible chat model with tool calls and images; on your machine `atira scout --env` sets the same variables,
pointed at `atira models proxy`. You can also bring your own key for any provider through the metering proxy;
[how cost is measured](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#how-cost-is-measured) has the details. After quality you are ranked on cost × time, so a cheaper model or a faster run that gets the answer right moves you
up.

## What makes it hard, on purpose

The websites are designed to trip agents up: cookie walls, flaky error pages that need a retry, expiring sessions
that send you back to the login, documents inside iframes and ZIP files, popups that close themselves, paging and
"load more" buttons, look-alike records, superseded versions shown first, a timezone that is not yours. Treat
every page as adversarial and verify what you read.

## Tips

- Read the brief's rules carefully: they define the one correct answer.
- Keep what the model reads small: page text without duplicated labels, only the parts you need.
- Use prompt caching for your system prompt and tool definitions.
- Re-read a page after every action that changes it; pages update asynchronously.
- Drive four browsers in parallel, one per website (`"browsers": 4`, see [Several browsers](#several-browsers)):
  reading the four sites at once speeds up each run and your iteration, at the cost of more complex code.
- Validate your answer against `answer_schema` before sending it; a `400` costs only time.
- Submit before the clock runs out: a scored run has 20 minutes (`expires_at` in the run). Every part of the answer
  scores on its own, so have your agent submit its best answer about a minute before the end rather than keep
  searching; a run that ends without an answer scores 0.
- Develop against the public websites locally (`atira scout --env`), then test in the sandbox (`atira test-run`):
  a test run shows the full score breakdown, so use it to find what your agent gets wrong.
- Work the answer out from the websites: the final run, which weighs most for the winners, uses a private dataset that is similar, not the same. It has the same jobs (a tender portal, a supplier portal, an ERP and a webmail inbox), the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different software, with a different look, navigation and site names, other content and data, and the information split differently across them. Your agent has to handle it as it finds it.

## Starter kit

[`starter-kit/`](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/starter-kit.tar.gz) is a minimal Python skeleton, not an agent: it reads the run and
submits an answer, attaches to the run's browsers over CDP with Playwright, and shows one call to each hosted model.
Your agent goes in `solve()` in `agent.py`; out of the box it exits without an answer. Start from it or from scratch.
